title: Effects of landscape on soundscape perception: Soundwalks in city parks.
authors: Liu, J., Kang, J., Behm, H. et al., 2014
research_question: 1) characterisation of soundscape perception in city parks using various parameters; 2) analysis of the effects of the physical composition of the visual landscape on soundscape perception in city parks in view of on-site landscape composition and local landscape spatial pattern; 3) exploration of methods to combine soundscape information into applied landscape management.

participants.description: 7 soundwalk observers (4 female, 3 male, average age 25±1.5 years, normal hearing abilities) and 580 general public park users in Xiamen, China.
participants.recruitment: Soundwalk observers were trained; general public participated in a supplementary questionnaire survey.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Five public city parks in Xiamen, China (Bailuzhou (west), Huli, Haiwan, Nanhu, Zhongshan). Six sampled sites were chosen in each park along main visitor paths.

Panoramic landscape photos (8-10 photos per site) shot horizontally at 1.2m height using Canon EOS 5D Mark II. Used to calculate percentages of landscape elements (vegetation, water, buildings, pavement, furniture, sky).

Digitalized land cover maps (buildings, roads, water areas) from IKONOS satellite images and Google Earth data. Vegetation density from SPOT satellite images (NDVI). Landscape spatial pattern indices (PLAND, LPI, LSI, COHESION) calculated for 175m radius buffer areas around each sampled site.

mechanisms: Masking effects of anthropogenic sounds (human, mechanical, music) on natural sounds (biological, geophysical).
Human activity patterns influenced by environmental features (e.g., seeking shade in hot climates) affecting sound presence.
Specific sound source locations (e.g., loudspeakers in vegetation, lawn mowing schedules).
Environmental openness/exposure affecting perception of geophysical sounds (e.g., wind).
Attractiveness of landscape features (e.g., complex building shapes, water areas) drawing more people and associated sounds.
Traffic load on roads influencing traffic sound levels.
Vocal organisms compensating for masking effects of traffic sound by increasing song frequency or amplitude.
Landscape configuration affecting sound transmission routes.
Visual aesthetic and functional aspects of the landscape influencing overall soundscape perception and preference for specific sound categories.
implementation_implications: Introduce more natural sounds into city parks to improve soundscape quality.
Prioritize physical composition of visual landscape in favor of natural sounds in urban landscape management.
Manage landscape according to positive or negative relationships of different landscape indices with perception parameters of different sounds.
Consider the spatial arrangement of different landscape elements in landscape and urban planning/design to improve soundscape quality.
Incorporate soundscape information derived from the general public as a supplement to 'objective' soundwalk data.
Consider buildings, vegetation, and sky as key effective landscape elements in future studies, especially sky.
Introduce water features into parks to potentially increase soundscape diversity and attractiveness to park users.

limitations: Limitations of photographic techniques for measuring landscape composition (e.g., conical projection, lens zoom, camera vertical angle, distance from lens affecting element size, visual thresholds, distortion of perspective).
Soundscape information from soundwalks is confined to certain sites and time periods and limited to a small group of observers, which differs from the general public's experience.
Landscape indices may not be predictive for all sound categories (e.g., mechanical sounds due to their unstable nature).
The scale of the study (175m radius) may not be well related to sounds beyond that scale, necessitating consideration of scaling effects in future studies.
Not all developed landscape indices were tested as suitable soundscape indicators.
Aural-visual interactions could be biased as observers were requested to focus on detecting sounds during soundwalks and did not perceive the surrounding landscape at the same time.
